statement: Let $X$ be a connected nonsingular complex [algebraic variety](c:algebraic-variety). The functor $Y\mapsto Y^{an}$ is an equivalence from the finite étale covers of $X$ to the finite [covering spaces](c:covering-space) of the [analytic space](c:analytic-space) $X^{an}$.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is an [algebraic variety](c:algebraic-variety) over $\mathbb{C}$, separated and of finite type.
$X$ is connected and nonsingular.

conclusion: Analytification is an equivalence between finite étale covers of $X$ and finite covering spaces of $X^{an}$, so the [étale fundamental group](c:etale-fundamental-group) of $X$ is the profinite completion of $\pi_1(X^{an})$.

proofs.name: Grothendieck's proof via GAGA
proofs.slogan: Compare covers through full faithfulness from connectedness, then extend analytic covers over a compactification and algebraize them by GAGA.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof for connected nonsingular $X$; the connectedness, extension and GAGA results rest on the cited work. SGA 1 proves it for every normal $X$, and for curves it shows that every compact Riemann surface is algebraic.

roles.why: Finite type and separatedness give the analytic space and the compactification.
Normality makes the extension across the boundary unique, and connectedness makes the fundamental groups defined.

steps.slogan: Show that analytification is fully faithful on finite étale covers.
steps.detail: A connected scheme $Z$ of finite type over $\mathbb{C}$ has connected $Z^{an}$ (SGA 1, XII, 2.4), so the components of $Z^{an}$ are the analytifications of those of $Z$. An analytic morphism $Y^{an}\to Y'^{an}$ over $X^{an}$ has a graph that is open and closed in $(Y\times_X Y')^{an}$. So the graph is a union of components, hence algebraic.

steps.slogan: Compactify $X$ to a proper normal variety $\bar X$ with boundary $D$.
steps.detail: By Nagata's theorem $X$ is open and dense in a proper variety. Its normalization $\bar X$ is proper and normal, and $X=\bar X\setminus D$ for a closed set $D$ of smaller dimension. Properness is what allows GAGA in step 4.

steps.slogan: Extend a finite covering of $X^{an}$ across $D$ as a normal analytic space.
steps.detail: For a finite covering $E\to X^{an}$, the Grauert-Remmert extension theorem gives a normal analytic space $\bar E$ with a finite map $\bar E\to\bar X^{an}$ that restricts to $E$ over $X^{an}$. The extension is unique, and it may branch along $D$.

steps.slogan: Make the finite analytic cover algebraic with GAGA.
steps.detail: Since $\bar X$ is proper, the coherent analytic algebra $\pi_*\mathcal{O}_{\bar E}$ is the analytification of a coherent algebra on $\bar X$. Its relative spectrum is a finite $\bar X$-scheme $\bar Y$ with $\bar Y^{an}=\bar E$. Restricting over $X$ gives a finite étale $Y$ with $Y^{an}\cong E$.

steps.slogan: Compare the fundamental groups of the two categories of covers.
steps.detail: Finite coverings of the connected, locally simply connected $X^{an}$ correspond to finite $\pi_1(X^{an})$-sets. Finite étale covers of $X$ correspond to finite continuous $\pi_1^{et}(X)$-sets. The equivalence of steps 1 to 4 matches them, so $\pi_1^{et}(X)$ is the profinite completion.

concepts.c:algebraic-variety: The variety $X$ is the base whose covers are compared.
concepts.c:covering-space: Finite covering spaces of $X^{an}$ form the target category.
concepts.c:analytic-space: Both $X^{an}$ and the extended cover $\bar E$ are analytic spaces.
concepts.c:etale-fundamental-group: The equivalence of categories identifies this group with a profinite completion.

source.ref: A. Grothendieck and M. Raynaud, Revêtements étales et groupe fondamental (SGA 1), Exposé XII, Théorème 5.1, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 224, Springer, 1971
source.note: Full faithfulness uses connectedness of analytifications (XII 2.4); essential surjectivity uses the Grauert-Remmert extension theorem (Math. Ann. 136, 1958) and GAGA.

statement: A finite undirected [graph](c:graph) $G$, with parallel edges allowed, has a [strong orientation](c:strong-orientation) if and only if $G$ is [connected](c:connected-graph) and has no bridge, that is, if and only if $G$ is [2-edge-connected](c:2-edge-connected-graph).

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a finite undirected [graph](c:graph); loops and parallel edges are allowed.

conclusion: The edges of $G$ can be oriented so that every vertex reaches every other vertex along directed edges exactly when $G$ is connected and every edge lies on a cycle (a bridge is an edge on no cycle).

proofs.name: Ear by ear
proofs.slogan: Show necessity by cutting a bridge, and build a strong orientation by adding ears to a strongly connected subgraph.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for finite graphs with loops and parallel edges. A one-vertex graph is connected and strongly oriented with no edges.

roles.why: Finiteness stops the process, and the edges of $G$ supply the cycles used in the ears.

steps.slogan: Show that a strong orientation forces $G$ to be connected and bridgeless.
steps.detail: A directed path between any two vertices makes $G$ connected. Suppose an edge $e=uv$ is a bridge. Then $G-e$ has sides $A\ni u$ and $B\ni v$, and $e$ is the only edge between them. The orientation of $e$ points from one side to the other, so no directed path returns, which contradicts strong connectivity.

steps.slogan: Find an [ear](c:ear-decomposition) that leaves the current strongly connected subgraph $H$ and returns to it.
steps.detail: Let $H$ be an oriented subgraph in which every vertex reaches every other, for example one vertex. If $V(H)\ne V(G)$, connectedness gives an edge $e=uv$ with $u\in V(H)$ and $v\notin V(H)$. The edge $e$ lies on a cycle. Follow the cycle from $u$ through $e$ until it first meets $V(H)$ again, at $w$ (possibly $w=u$). This path $P$ is an ear with inner vertices outside $H$.

steps.slogan: Orient the ear from $u$ to $w$ and check that $H\cup P$ stays strongly connected.
steps.detail: Each new vertex of $P$ is reached from $u$ along $P$ and reaches $w$ along $P$. Since $H$ is strongly connected, each new vertex reaches every vertex of $H$ through $w$ and is reached from every vertex of $H$ through $u$. So $H\cup P$ is strongly connected.

steps.slogan: Orient every remaining edge with both ends in $H$ in any direction.
steps.detail: If $e=uv$ has both ends in $V(H)$, orient it from $u$ to $v$. The path from $v$ to $u$ inside $H$ closes it into a cycle, so the larger subgraph is still strongly connected. A loop may take either direction.

steps.slogan: Repeat the two moves until $H$ contains all vertices and edges, and join both directions.
steps.detail: Each round adds an edge, so the process stops. It stops only when no vertex lies outside $H$, since otherwise an ear exists, and no edge is unused. Then $H$ is a strong orientation of $G$. With step 1 this proves the equivalence.

concepts.c:graph: The proof builds an orientation of the edges of a finite graph.
concepts.c:strong-orientation: The goal is an orientation that is strongly connected.
concepts.c:connected-graph: Connectedness is necessary, and it supplies an edge leaving $H$.
concepts.c:2-edge-connected-graph: Having no bridge puts every edge on a cycle, which gives the ears.
concepts.c:ear-decomposition: The steps add ears one by one, which is an ear decomposition of $G$.

source.note: The ear argument of H. E. Robbins, A theorem on graphs, with an application to a problem of traffic control, American Mathematical Monthly 46 (1939), 281-283.

statement: Let $X=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb{H}$ be a compact [hyperbolic surface](c:hyperbolic-surface) with $\Gamma$ torsion free, and let $\tfrac14+r_n^2$ be the eigenvalues of its [Laplace operator](c:laplace-operator). For $h$ even, holomorphic and $O((1+|r|)^{-2-\varepsilon})$ on $|\mathrm{Im}\,r|\le\tfrac12+\varepsilon$, with $g(u)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}}h(r)e^{-iru}\,dr$: $\sum_n h(r_n)=\frac{\mathrm{Area}(X)}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}}r\,h(r)\tanh(\pi r)\,dr+\sum_{\gamma}\frac{\ell(\gamma_0)}{2\sinh(\ell(\gamma)/2)}\,g(\ell(\gamma))$. Here $\gamma$ runs over the hyperbolic [conjugacy classes](c:conjugacy-class) of $\Gamma$, that is, over the oriented [closed geodesics](c:closed-geodesic) of $X$ with all multiples, and $\ell(\gamma_0)$ is the length of the primitive geodesic below $\gamma$.

hypotheses.text: $\Gamma$ is a torsion-free cocompact [Fuchsian group](c:fuchsian-group), so $X=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb{H}$ is a compact [hyperbolic surface](c:hyperbolic-surface).
The function $h$ is even and holomorphic on $|\mathrm{Im}\,r|\le\tfrac12+\varepsilon$, with $h(r)=O((1+|r|)^{-2-\varepsilon})$ there.

conclusion: The sum of $h$ over the spectral parameters $r_n$ equals an area term plus a sum over the lengths of closed geodesics.

proofs.name: Integrate the automorphic kernel over the diagonal
proofs.slogan: Periodize a point-pair invariant over $\Gamma$, then compute the trace of the resulting kernel once spectrally and once through conjugacy classes.
proofs.scope: An outline of Selberg's proof for torsion-free cocompact $\Gamma$; the Selberg transform and the orbital integrals rest on the cited work. The family includes the trace formulas with elliptic and parabolic terms and the Arthur-Selberg formula.

roles.why: Compactness gives a discrete spectrum and a compact operator, and torsion freeness leaves only identity and hyperbolic classes.
The decay of $h$ makes the kernel and both sides converge, and evenness lets $h$ be a Selberg transform.

steps.slogan: Build a radial kernel $k$ whose Selberg transform is $h$.
steps.detail: A point-pair invariant $k(z,w)=k(u(z,w))$ acts on every eigenfunction with eigenvalue $\tfrac14+r^2$ as multiplication by $h(r)$. The kernel is recovered from $h$ through $g$ by the Abel transform and its inversion (Selberg-Harish-Chandra transform).

steps.slogan: Periodize $k$ over $\Gamma$ to an automorphic kernel on $X$.
steps.detail: The sum $K(z,w)=\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma}k(z,\gamma w)$ converges. Since $X$ is compact, the integral operator of $K$ is a compact self-adjoint operator on $L^2(X)$.

steps.slogan: Expand $K$ in orthonormal eigenfunctions and integrate over the diagonal.
steps.detail: The eigenfunctions $\phi_n$ are [automorphic forms](c:automorphic-form) of weight $0$ for $\Gamma$, and $K(z,w)=\sum_n h(r_n)\phi_n(z)\overline{\phi_n(w)}$. Integrating $K(z,z)$ over a fundamental domain $F$ gives $\sum_n h(r_n)$; the decay of $h$ makes the series converge.

steps.slogan: Group the terms of $K(z,z)$ by conjugacy classes of $\Gamma$.
steps.detail: $\int_F K(z,z)\,d\mu=\sum_{\{\gamma\}}\int_{\Gamma_\gamma\backslash\mathbb{H}}k(z,\gamma z)\,d\mu(z)$, where $\Gamma_\gamma$ is the centralizer. As $\Gamma$ is cocompact and torsion free, the classes are the identity and the hyperbolic classes.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the identity term and each hyperbolic orbital integral.
steps.detail: The identity gives $\mathrm{Area}(X)\,k(0)=\frac{\mathrm{Area}(X)}{4\pi}\int r\,h(r)\tanh(\pi r)\,dr$ by Selberg inversion. A hyperbolic class conjugate to $z\mapsto e^{\ell}z$ has centralizer generated by the primitive root, and unfolding along its axis gives $\ell(\gamma_0)\,g(\ell)/(2\sinh(\ell/2))$.

steps.slogan: Equate the spectral and the geometric expressions for the trace of the kernel.
steps.detail: Both steps 3 and 5 compute $\int_F K(z,z)\,d\mu$. Setting them equal gives the stated identity.

concepts.c:hyperbolic-surface: The surface $X$ carries the Laplacian whose spectrum is summed.
concepts.c:laplace-operator: Its eigenvalues $\tfrac14+r_n^2$ are the spectral side of the formula.
concepts.c:conjugacy-class: Conjugacy classes of $\Gamma$ index the terms of the geometric side.
concepts.c:closed-geodesic: Hyperbolic classes correspond to closed geodesics, whose lengths enter the formula.
concepts.c:fuchsian-group: The group $\Gamma$ defines the surface and the sum over its elements.
concepts.c:automorphic-form: The eigenfunctions expand the automorphic kernel.

source.ref: A. Selberg, Harmonic analysis and discontinuous groups in weakly symmetric Riemannian spaces with applications to Dirichlet series, Journal of the Indian Mathematical Society 20 (1956), 47-87
source.note: Textbook form: H. Iwaniec, Spectral Methods of Automorphic Forms, Chapter 10, and D. Hejhal, The Selberg trace formula for PSL(2,R), Volume 1, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 548, 1976.

statement: For integers $k,n\ge1$, the [homotopy group](c:homotopy-group-of-spheres) $\pi_n(S^k)$ is finite, except when $n=k$ or when $k$ is even and $n=2k-1$. In those cases it is infinite: $\pi_k(S^k)\cong\mathbb{Z}$ and $\pi_{2k-1}(S^k)\cong\mathbb{Z}\oplus(\text{finite})$.

hypotheses.text: $k$ and $n$ are integers with $k\ge1$ and $n\ge1$.

conclusion: The group $\pi_n(S^k)$ is finite outside the two exceptional families, and infinite of rank one on them.

proofs.name: Serre classes and rational homotopy of spheres
proofs.slogan: Use Serre classes of abelian groups, then compare each sphere with an Eilenberg-MacLane space whose fibre is rationally an odd sphere or trivial.
proofs.scope: An outline of Serre's proof for spheres; the mod-$\mathcal{C}$ theorems rest on the cited work. Serre's other finiteness results, for homotopy groups of simply connected finite-type spaces and for cohomology of coherent sheaves, are not proved here.

roles.why: The indices select the odd case, the even case and the two exceptional families.

steps.slogan: Show that the homotopy groups of a sphere are finitely generated.
steps.detail: The finitely generated abelian groups form a Serre class. The mod-$\mathcal{C}$ version of the Hurewicz theorem, driven by the [Serre spectral sequence](c:serre-spectral-sequence) of the path fibration, gives finitely generated homotopy groups for a simply connected space with finitely generated homology. Apply it to $S^k$ ($k\ge2$).

steps.slogan: Compare an odd sphere $S^k$ with $K(\mathbb{Z},k)$ to get finite groups above degree $k$.
steps.detail: For odd $k$ the map $S^k\to K(\mathbb{Z},k)$ is a rational cohomology isomorphism, since both have $\Lambda[\iota_k]$. Its homotopy fibre $F$ is $k$-connected with finite homology, so $\pi_n(F)$ is finite. As $\pi_nK(\mathbb{Z},k)=0$ for $n>k$, the group $\pi_n(S^k)\cong\pi_n(F)$ is finite for $n>k$.

steps.slogan: Show that the fibre for an even sphere $S^{2m}$ is rationally the odd sphere $S^{4m-1}$.
steps.detail: Let $F$ be the fibre of $S^{2m}\to K(\mathbb{Z},2m)$, which is $2m$-connected. In the Serre spectral sequence, $H^*(K;\mathbb{Q})=\mathbb{Q}[\iota]$ and $H^*(S^{2m};\mathbb{Q})=\mathbb{Q}[\iota]/\iota^2$ force $H^*(F;\mathbb{Q})=\Lambda[y_{4m-1}]$ with $dy=\iota^2$.

steps.slogan: Compare $F$ with $S^{4m-1}$ by a map that is a rational homology isomorphism.
steps.detail: By the mod-$\mathcal{C}$ Hurewicz theorem, $\pi_{4m-1}(F)\cong\mathbb{Z}\oplus(\text{finite})$, so some map $S^{4m-1}\to F$ is a rational equivalence. The mod-$\mathcal{C}$ Whitehead theorem and the odd case then make $\pi_n(F)$ finite for $n\ne4m-1$.

steps.slogan: Read off $\pi_n(S^{2m})\cong\pi_n(F)$ for $n>2m$ and collect all cases.
steps.detail: Since $\pi_nK(\mathbb{Z},2m)=0$ for $n>2m$, we get $\pi_n(S^{2m})\cong\pi_n(F)$ for $n>2m$: finite for $n\ne4m-1$ and of rank one for $n=4m-1$. Also $\pi_k(S^k)\cong\mathbb{Z}$ by Hurewicz, $\pi_n(S^k)=0$ for $n<k$, and the odd case covers all odd $k$.

concepts.c:homotopy-group-of-spheres: These groups are the objects whose finiteness is proved.
concepts.c:serre-spectral-sequence: It computes the rational cohomology of the fibre and gives finite generation.

source.ref: J.-P. Serre, Groupes d'homotopie et classes de groupes abéliens, Annals of Mathematics (2) 58 (1953), 258-294
source.note: Serre classes, the mod-C Hurewicz and Whitehead theorems, and the computation for spheres are all in this paper.

statement: In univalent type theory, let $\mathcal{X}$ be a univalent category and $(P,H)$ a notion of structure on $\mathcal{X}$. For structured objects $(x,\alpha)$ and $(y,\beta)$, the canonical map from identifications $(x,\alpha)=(y,\beta)$ to structure [isomorphisms](c:isomorphism) $(x,\alpha)\cong(y,\beta)$ is an equivalence of types.

hypotheses.text: $\mathcal{X}$ is a category in which $\mathrm{idtoiso}\colon(x=y)\to(x\cong y)$ is an equivalence for all objects $x,y$.

$(P,H)$ is a notion of structure: $H_{\alpha\beta}(f)$ is a mere proposition, identities and composites are homomorphisms, and structures $\alpha,\beta$ on one object with $1_x$ a homomorphism both ways are equal.

conclusion: Identifications of structured objects are the same as [isomorphisms](c:isomorphism) of structures, so structured objects that are isomorphic are equal.

proofs.name: Path induction on the base category
proofs.slogan: Reduce identity of structured objects to identity of base objects with a transport, then to isomorphisms by univalence.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; the proof uses only that $\mathcal{X}$ is univalent. Under the [univalence axiom](c:univalence-axiom) the categories of sets, groups and rings are univalent, so isomorphic groups are equal.

roles.why: Univalence of the base category replaces paths between objects by isomorphisms.
The axioms make homomorphism conditions propositions and make structures on one object equal when they are isomorphic by $1_x$.

steps.slogan: Describe identifications of pairs as a path plus a transport.
steps.detail: By the characterization of paths in $\Sigma$-types, $((x,\alpha)=(y,\beta))\simeq\Sigma(p:x=y).\,p_*(\alpha)=\beta$.

steps.slogan: Replace paths $x=y$ by isomorphisms $x\cong y$ using univalence of $\mathcal{X}$.
steps.detail: Since $\mathrm{idtoiso}$ is an equivalence, reindexing the $\Sigma$-type along it gives $\Sigma(f:x\cong y).\,(\mathrm{idtoiso}^{-1}f)_*(\alpha)=\beta$.

steps.slogan: Show that $p_*(\alpha)=\beta$ holds exactly when $\mathrm{idtoiso}(p)$ is a homomorphism both ways.
steps.detail: By path induction on $p$ it suffices to take $p=\mathrm{refl}_x$, where the claim reads $(\alpha=\beta)\simeq H_{\alpha\beta}(1_x)\times H_{\beta\alpha}(1_x)$. The right side implies the left by axiom (v), and the left implies the right since $H_{\alpha\alpha}(1_x)$ holds. Both are mere propositions, so they are equivalent.

steps.slogan: Assemble the equivalences into one equivalence of identity types.
steps.detail: Steps 1 to 3 give $((x,\alpha)=(y,\beta))\simeq\Sigma(f:x\cong y).\,H_{\alpha\beta}(f)\times H_{\beta\alpha}(f^{-1})$. The right side is the type of isomorphisms $(x,\alpha)\cong(y,\beta)$ of structures. Tracing the map shows that it is the canonical one.

concepts.c:isomorphism: Isomorphisms of structures are the type that identifications are shown equivalent to.
concepts.c:univalence-axiom: It makes the standard categories of sets, groups and rings univalent, which gives the examples.

source.note: The proof of the structure identity principle in The Univalent Foundations Program, Homotopy Type Theory: Univalent Foundations of Mathematics, Institute for Advanced Study, 2013, Section 9.8.

statement: The category of topological spaces has a [model structure](c:model-category) whose weak equivalences are the [homotopy equivalences](c:homotopy-equivalence), whose [fibrations](c:fibration) are the Hurewicz fibrations, and whose cofibrations are the [closed cofibrations](c:closed-cofibration) in the sense of Hurewicz.

hypotheses.text: $\mathbf{Top}$ is the category of all topological spaces and continuous maps.

conclusion: The three classes of maps satisfy the axioms of a closed model category.

proofs.name: Strøm's lemmas and path-space factorization
proofs.slogan: Prove the two lifting axioms from Strøm's and Dold's lemmas, and build the two factorizations from mapping cylinders and mapping path spaces.
proofs.scope: An outline of Strøm's published proof; the two lemmas and the point-set check that the factorization maps are closed cofibrations rest on the cited work.

roles.why: The category of all spaces has the limits, colimits, mapping cylinders and path spaces that the factorizations use.

steps.slogan: Check limits, colimits, two-out-of-three and retract closure of the three classes.
steps.detail: $\mathbf{Top}$ has all small limits and colimits. Homotopy equivalences are the maps that become isomorphisms in the homotopy category, so they satisfy two-out-of-three and are closed under retracts. Hurewicz fibrations and closed cofibrations are defined by lifting properties, and both are closed under retracts.

steps.slogan: Show that a closed cofibration that is a homotopy equivalence lifts against fibrations.
steps.detail: By Strøm's lemma such a map $A\to X$ is the inclusion of a strong deformation retract. The deformation and the homotopy lifting property of a Hurewicz fibration then solve every lifting square.

steps.slogan: Show that a Hurewicz fibration that is a homotopy equivalence lifts against closed cofibrations.
steps.detail: By Dold's theorem such a map $p\colon E\to B$ is a fibre homotopy equivalence, so it has a section $s$ with $sp\simeq1$ over $B$. Homotopy extension along a closed cofibration then solves every lifting square.

steps.slogan: Factor a map into a trivial closed cofibration followed by a Hurewicz fibration.
steps.detail: Use a mapping path space whose paths carry a length. The inclusion of $X$ is a strong deformation retract and the zero set of a function $u\colon P_f\to[0,1]$, so Strøm's criterion makes it a closed cofibration and a homotopy equivalence. The end-point map $P_f\to Y$ is a Hurewicz fibration.

steps.slogan: Factor a map into a closed cofibration followed by a trivial fibration.
steps.detail: Write $f=r\circ i$ with $i\colon X\to M_f$ the inclusion into the mapping cylinder, a closed cofibration, and $r\colon M_f\to Y$ a homotopy equivalence. Factor $r=q\circ j$ by the previous step. Then $q$ is a fibration and a homotopy equivalence, and $j\circ i$ is a closed cofibration.

steps.slogan: Collect steps 1 to 5 as the axioms of a closed model category.
steps.detail: Step 1 gives the limit, colimit, two-out-of-three and retract axioms. Steps 2 and 3 give the two lifting axioms. Steps 4 and 5 give the two factorization axioms.

concepts.c:model-category: The proof checks the axioms of a model category for the three classes.
concepts.c:homotopy-equivalence: These maps are the weak equivalences, and the homotopy category makes them satisfy two-out-of-three.
concepts.c:fibration: Hurewicz fibrations are the fibrations, and their homotopy lifting gives the first lifting axiom.
concepts.c:closed-cofibration: Closed cofibrations are the cofibrations, and homotopy extension gives the second lifting axiom.

source.ref: A. Strøm, The homotopy category is a homotopy category, Archiv der Mathematik 23 (1972), 435-441
source.note: The lemmas come from Strøm, Note on cofibrations II, Math. Scand. 22 (1968), 130-142, and Dold, Partitions of unity in the theory of fibrations, Ann. of Math. 78 (1963), 223-255.

statement: Let $f\colon M\to N$ be an [embedding](c:embedding) of $L$-structures. Suppose that whenever $\varphi(\bar x,y)$ is a formula, $\bar m\in M$ and $N\models\varphi(f\bar m,a)$ for some $a\in N$, there is $b\in M$ with $N\models\varphi(f\bar m,f b)$. Then $f$ is an [elementary embedding](c:elementary-embedding): $N\models\varphi(f\bar m)$ iff $M\models\varphi(\bar m)$ for every [first-order](c:first-order-logic) formula $\varphi$.

hypotheses.text: $f\colon M\to N$ is an [embedding](c:embedding) of $L$-structures; for a [substructure](c:substructure) $M\subseteq N$ it is the inclusion.
For every formula $\varphi(\bar x,y)$, tuple $\bar m\in M$ and $a\in N$ with $N\models\varphi(f\bar m,a)$, some $b\in M$ has $N\models\varphi(f\bar m,fb)$.

conclusion: The embedding $f$ is elementary: it preserves and reflects every first-order formula.

formal.difference: mathlib states the witness condition for formulas with one extra bound variable and concludes for formulas with free variables $\mathrm{Fin}\,n$; this is the same statement. The declaration proves only this direction, and the converse (an elementary embedding satisfies the condition) is not part of it.

proofs.name: Induction on formulas
proofs.slogan: Prove the equivalence for all formulas by induction, where the witness condition handles the quantifier step.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for any language $L$. The converse, that every elementary embedding satisfies the condition, is immediate and not part of this proof.

roles.why: Injectivity and the reflection of relations settle the atomic case.
The witness condition gives the hard direction of the quantifier step.

steps.slogan: Strengthen the claim to formulas with bound variables, then induct on formulas.
steps.detail: It suffices to prove, for every $n$, every formula $\varphi$ with $n$ bound variables and every $\bar m\in M^n$, that $N\models\varphi(f\bar m)$ iff $M\models\varphi(\bar m)$. Formulas with free variables reduce to this case by relabeling the free variables as bound ones.

steps.slogan: Check equalities and relations, using that $f$ is an embedding.
steps.detail: Terms commute with $f$: $f(t^M(\bar m))=t^N(f\bar m)$. So $f$ preserves and reflects equalities because it is injective, and relations because an embedding reflects them.

steps.slogan: Pass falsity and implication through the induction hypotheses.
steps.detail: Falsity fails in both structures. For $\varphi\to\psi$, the induction hypotheses for $\varphi$ and $\psi$ give the same truth value in $M$ at $\bar m$ and in $N$ at $f\bar m$.

steps.slogan: Prove the case $\forall y\,\varphi$ in both directions, using the witness condition.
steps.detail:
If $N\models orall y\,\varphi(f ar m,y)$, take $y=fb$ and use the induction hypothesis to get $M\models orall y\,\varphi( ar m,y)$. Conversely, if $N\models
eg\varphi(f ar m,a)$ for some $a$, the condition for $
eg\varphi$ gives $b\in M$ with $N\models
eg\varphi(f ar m,fb)$, so $M\models
eg\varphi( ar m,b)$ by induction.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $f$ is an elementary embedding.
steps.detail: The three cases cover all formulas, so the equivalence holds for every formula with bound variables, and by step 1 for every formula with free variables.

concepts.c:embedding: Its injectivity and reflection of relations give the atomic case.
concepts.c:elementary-embedding: The theorem says that $f$ is elementary, which the induction proves.
concepts.c:first-order-logic: The induction runs over the construction of first-order formulas.
concepts.c:substructure: The inclusion of a substructure is the standard case of the embedding.

source.note: mathlib recurses on BoundedFormula, using HomClass.realize_term and map_rel for atoms, and realize_all, realize_not and the witness hypothesis for the quantifier.

statement: Let $A$ and $C$ be the end points of a [diameter](c:diameter) of a [circle](c:circle) with centre $O$, and let $B$ be a point. Then $\angle ABC=\pi/2$ if and only if $B$ lies on the circle.

hypotheses.text: $AC$ is a [diameter](c:diameter) of the [circle](c:circle) with centre $O$, so $O$ is the midpoint of $AC$.

conclusion: The angle $\angle ABC$ is a right angle exactly when $B$ is on the circle.

formal.difference: The declaration works in any Euclidean affine space, not only the plane, and states the equivalence for every point $B$. For $B=A$ or $B=C$ the angle is $\pi/2$ by the convention for a zero vector.

proofs.name: Inner product through the centre
proofs.slogan: Write the angle condition as a vanishing inner product and expand it through the centre to get $|OB|^2-r^2$.
proofs.scope: The whole equivalence, in any dimension. For $B=A$ or $B=C$ the angle is $\pi/2$ by the zero-vector convention; Euclid's theorem is the case of distinct points.

roles.why: The midpoint property of the centre cancels the cross terms, and the circle gives the radius.

steps.slogan: Turn the right-angle condition into an inner product condition.
steps.detail: The angle $\angle ABC$ is the angle between $A-B$ and $C-B$. It equals $\pi/2$ iff $\langle A-B,\,C-B\rangle=0$. A zero vector gives the same on both sides by convention.

steps.slogan: Write both vectors with the centre $O$ as base point.
steps.detail: $A-B=(A-O)+(O-B)$ and $C-B=(C-O)+(O-B)$. So the inner product expands into four terms.

steps.slogan: Use $A-O=-(C-O)$ to collapse the four terms.
steps.detail: Since $O$ is the midpoint of $AC$, $A-O=-(C-O)$. The two cross terms cancel by symmetry of the inner product. This leaves $\langle A-B,\,C-B\rangle=|O-B|^2-|C-O|^2$.

steps.slogan: Compare the distances $|OB|$ and $|OC|$ to the radius.
steps.detail: The radius is $r=|OC|$. So the inner product vanishes iff $|OB|^2=r^2$, that is iff $B$ lies on the circle.

concepts.c:diameter: The diameter makes $O$ the midpoint of $AC$, which collapses the expansion.
concepts.c:circle: The right-angle condition is shown equivalent to $B$ lying on this circle.

source.note: mathlib rewrites the angle with inner_eq_zero_iff_angle_eq_pi_div_two, expands through the centre with inner_add_left and inner_add_right, and compares dist to the radius.

proofs.name: Euclid's isosceles triangles
proofs.slogan: Split the angle at $B$ by the radius $OB$ and add the base angles of the two isosceles triangles.
proofs.scope: Only the direction that a point $B\ne A,C$ on the circle gives a right angle, in the plane. This is Euclid's argument, Elements III.31.

roles.why: The centre lies on $AC$ and is equidistant from all three points, which gives the two isosceles triangles.

steps.slogan: Join $B$ to $O$ and note that $OA=OB=OC$.
steps.detail: Let $B$ be on the circle, distinct from $A$ and $C$. The three segments are radii. Since $O$ lies on $AC$ between $A$ and $C$, the ray $BO$ lies inside $\angle ABC$, so $\angle ABC=\angle ABO+\angle OBC$.

steps.slogan: Equate the base angles of the isosceles triangles $OAB$ and $OBC$.
steps.detail: As $OA=OB$, $\angle OAB=\angle OBA=\alpha$. As $OB=OC$, $\angle OBC=\angle OCB=\gamma$.

steps.slogan: Add the angles of triangle $ABC$ to get $\alpha+\gamma=\pi/2$.
steps.detail: The angles of $ABC$ are $\alpha$ at $A$, $\gamma$ at $C$ and $\alpha+\gamma$ at $B$. Their sum is $\pi$, so $2(\alpha+\gamma)=\pi$ and $\angle ABC=\pi/2$.

concepts.c:diameter: The diameter puts $O$ on $AC$ between $A$ and $C$.
concepts.c:circle: Points of the circle are at the same distance from $O$.

statement: There is a constant $N_0$ such that every odd integer $N>N_0$ is a sum of three [prime numbers](c:prime-number).

hypotheses.text: $N$ is an odd integer.
$N$ is larger than some absolute constant $N_0$.

proofs.name: The circle method with Vinogradov's prime sums
proofs.slogan: Count representations by an integral over the circle, evaluate the major arcs, and bound the minor arcs by Vinogradov's estimate for prime exponential sums.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof; the Siegel-Walfisz theorem and the minor-arc bound of step 3 rest on the cited work. The proof gives the asymptotic $R(N)\sim\frac12\mathfrak{S}(N)N^2$ for the weighted count.

roles.why: For odd $N$ the singular series is positive, and for even $N$ it vanishes.
Largeness of $N$ makes the minor-arc error smaller than the main term.

steps.slogan: Write the weighted count of representations as an integral of an [exponential sum](c:exponential-sum).
steps.detail: Let $S(\alpha)=\sum_{n\le N}\Lambda(n)e(n\alpha)$. By orthogonality of $e(n\alpha)$, $R(N)=\sum_{n_1+n_2+n_3=N}\Lambda(n_1)\Lambda(n_2)\Lambda(n_3)=\int_0^1S(\alpha)^3e(-N\alpha)\,d\alpha$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the integral on major arcs by primes in arithmetic progressions.
steps.detail: Near $a/q$ with $q\le(\log N)^B$, the Siegel-Walfisz theorem gives $S(\alpha)\approx\frac{\mu(q)}{\varphi(q)}\sum_{n\le N}e(n\beta)$. The major arcs contribute $\tfrac12\mathfrak{S}(N)N^2(1+o(1))$, where $\mathfrak{S}(N)=\prod_{p\mid N}\bigl(1-\frac{1}{p^2-3p+3}\bigr)\prod_{p\nmid N}\bigl(1+\frac{1}{(p-1)^3}\bigr)\ge c>0$ for odd $N$.

steps.slogan: Bound $S(\alpha)$ uniformly on the minor arcs by Vinogradov's method.
steps.detail: Off the major arcs, Dirichlet approximation gives a rational with a moderate denominator. Vaughan's identity splits $S(\alpha)$ into type I and type II sums, which Cauchy-Schwarz bounds. The result is $\sup|S(\alpha)|\ll N(\log N)^{-A}$ for any fixed $A$.

steps.slogan: Bound the minor-arc integral with Parseval's identity.
steps.detail: The minor-arc integral is at most $\sup|S|\int_0^1|S|^2=\sup|S|\sum_{n\le N}\Lambda(n)^2\ll N^2(\log N)^{1-A}$. For $A>1$ this is $o(N^2)$.

steps.slogan: Compare the two arcs and return from weights to primes.
steps.detail: So $R(N)\ge cN^2$ for large odd $N$. Triples with a proper prime power contribute $O(N^{3/2}\log^3N)$. Hence some triple of primes sums to $N$.

concepts.c:prime-number: The three summands are primes, found through von Mangoldt weights.
concepts.c:exponential-sum: The sum $S(\alpha)$ over primes carries the whole argument.

source.ref: I. M. Vinogradov, Representation of an odd number as a sum of three primes, Doklady Akademii Nauk SSSR 15 (1937), 169-172
source.note: The modern proof with Vaughan's identity is in H. Davenport, Multiplicative Number Theory, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 74, Springer, chapters 25 and 26.

statement: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a small [Waldhausen category](c:waldhausen-category). Let $S_n\mathcal{C}$ be the category of chains of [cofibrations](c:cofibration) $0=A_0\rightarrowtail A_1\rightarrowtail\cdots\rightarrowtail A_n$ with chosen quotients $A_{ij}=A_j/A_i$. Then $S_\bullet\mathcal{C}$ is a [simplicial object](c:simplicial-object) in Waldhausen categories and exact functors, and $K(\mathcal{C})=\Omega|wS_\bullet\mathcal{C}|$ is an infinite loop space with $\pi_0K(\mathcal{C})=K_0(\mathcal{C})$.

hypotheses.text: $\mathcal{C}$ is a small [Waldhausen category](c:waldhausen-category): it has a zero object, cofibrations and weak equivalences that satisfy Waldhausen's axioms.

conclusion: The face and degeneracy maps of $S_\bullet\mathcal{C}$ are exact functors, and $\Omega|wS_\bullet\mathcal{C}|$ is an infinite loop space whose $\pi_0$ is the Grothendieck group $K_0(\mathcal{C})$.

proofs.name: Check the construction level by level
proofs.slogan: Check that each $S_n\mathcal{C}$ is Waldhausen and the operators are exact, then realize and iterate using additivity.
proofs.scope: An outline of Waldhausen's verification; the additivity theorem of step 5 rests on the cited work. The comparison with Quillen's Q-construction for exact categories is a separate theorem.

roles.why: The axioms of a Waldhausen category give the structure on $S_n\mathcal{C}$ and make the additivity theorem available.

steps.slogan: Describe $S_n\mathcal{C}$ as diagrams on the arrow category of $[n]$.
steps.detail: An object is a family $A_{ij}$ for $0\le i\le j\le n$ with $A_{ii}=0$, cofibrations $A_{ij}\rightarrowtail A_{ik}$, and cofibration sequences $A_{ij}\rightarrowtail A_{ik}\to A_{jk}$. It is the same as a chain of cofibrations with chosen quotients.

steps.slogan: Check that $S_n\mathcal{C}$ is a Waldhausen category.
steps.detail: A map $A\to B$ is a cofibration if all $A_{ij}\to B_{ij}$ and all $A_{ik}\cup_{A_{ij}}B_{ij}\to B_{ik}$ are cofibrations. Weak equivalences are objectwise. The pushout and gluing axioms of $\mathcal{C}$ give those of $S_n\mathcal{C}$.

steps.slogan: Check that faces and degeneracies are exact functors satisfying the simplicial identities.
steps.detail: Each operator $\theta\colon[m]\to[n]$ acts by restricting the diagram along $\theta$. Because $A_{aa}=0$, cofibration sequences stay cofibration sequences. Restriction preserves cofibrations, weak equivalences and the zero object, and composes strictly.

steps.slogan: Realize $wS_\bullet\mathcal{C}$ and read $\pi_0$ of its loop space.
steps.detail: Since $S_0\mathcal{C}$ is a point, $|wS_\bullet\mathcal{C}|$ is connected. Its $\pi_1$ is generated by the objects of $S_1\mathcal{C}\cong\mathcal{C}$, with $[A_{02}]=[A_{01}]+[A_{12}]$ from $S_2\mathcal{C}$ and $[A]=[A']$ for weak equivalences. This is $K_0(\mathcal{C})$.

steps.slogan: Iterate $S_\bullet$ to turn $\Omega|wS_\bullet\mathcal{C}|$ into an infinite loop space.
steps.detail: Since $S_\bullet\mathcal{C}$ is a simplicial Waldhausen category, apply $S_\bullet$ again. The spaces $K_m=|wS^{(m)}_\bullet\mathcal{C}|$ have maps $\Sigma K_m\to K_{m+1}$. By the additivity theorem $K_m\to\Omega K_{m+1}$ is an equivalence for $m\ge1$, so $K(\mathcal{C})=\Omega K_1$ is an infinite loop space.

concepts.c:waldhausen-category: The construction starts from this structure and keeps it at every level.
concepts.c:cofibration: Chains of cofibrations are the objects of $S_n\mathcal{C}$.
concepts.c:simplicial-object: The categories $S_n\mathcal{C}$ assemble into a simplicial object.

source.ref: F. Waldhausen, Algebraic K-theory of spaces, in Algebraic and Geometric Topology (New Brunswick, N.J., 1983), Lecture Notes in Mathematics 1126, Springer, 1985, pp. 318-419
source.note: The construction is in Section 1.3 and the additivity theorem in Section 1.4.

statement: Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional space over a field of characteristic not $2$ with a [nondegenerate](c:nondegenerate-form) [quadratic form](c:quadratic-form) $q$. Every [isometry](c:isometry) $\sigma\colon U\to W$ between subspaces of $V$ extends to an element of the [orthogonal group](c:orthogonal-group) of $(V,q)$.

hypotheses.text: $V$ is a finite-dimensional vector space over a field $k$ with $\mathrm{char}\,k\ne2$, with a [nondegenerate](c:nondegenerate-form) [quadratic form](c:quadratic-form) $q$.
$\sigma\colon U\to W$ is a linear bijection between subspaces of $V$ with $q(\sigma u)=q(u)$ for all $u\in U$, an [isometry](c:isometry).

proofs.name: Reflections and hyperbolic completion
proofs.slogan: Move vectors with reflections to extend isometries of nondegenerate subspaces, then reduce a general subspace to a nondegenerate one by adding hyperbolic partners.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for any subspace $U$, degenerate or not. In characteristic $2$ the statement needs alternating forms and is not proved here.

roles.why: Characteristic not $2$ gives reflections, and nondegeneracy gives orthogonal complements and hyperbolic partners.
Preservation of $q$ keeps radicals and nondegenerate parts, and makes the matched partners isometric.

steps.slogan: Move a vector to another vector of the same nonzero value with at most two [reflections](c:reflection-at-a-hyperplane).
steps.detail:
Let $B(x,y)=	frac12(q(x+y)-q(x)-q(y))$ and $q(x)=q(y)
e0$. Then $q(x-y)+q(x+y)=4q(x)
e0$. If $q(x-y)
e0$, the reflection in $x-y$ sends $x$ to $y$. Otherwise the reflection in $x+y$ sends $x$ to $-y$, and the reflection in $y$ sends $-y$ to $y$.

steps.slogan: Extend an isometric embedding of a nondegenerate subspace by induction on its dimension.
steps.detail: Take $e\in U$ with $q(e)\ne0$ and an isometry $\rho$ of $V$ with $\rho\sigma e=e$ (step 1). Then $\rho\sigma$ maps $U'=U\cap e^\perp$ isometrically into the nondegenerate space $e^\perp$. By induction it extends to $e^\perp$; add the identity on $\langle e\rangle$ and compose with $\rho^{-1}$.

steps.slogan: Place a general subspace $U$ inside a nondegenerate subspace $U_1$.
steps.detail: Write $U=R\oplus U_0$ with $R=U\cap U^\perp$ and $U_0$ nondegenerate. In the nondegenerate space $U_0^\perp$, the totally isotropic $R$ with basis $r_i$ has isotropic duals $r_i'$ spanning, with $R$, a hyperbolic space $H$. Then $U_1=U_0\perp H$ is nondegenerate and contains $U$.

steps.slogan: Extend $\sigma$ to an isometry $\sigma_1$ of $U_1$ by matching hyperbolic partners.
steps.detail: The radical of $W=\sigma(U)$ is $\sigma(R)$ and $\sigma(U_0)$ is nondegenerate. Repeat step 3 in $\sigma(U_0)^\perp$ to get duals $r_i''$ of $\sigma r_i$ and set $\sigma_1(r_i')=r_i''$. Then $\sigma_1$ is an isometry between nondegenerate subspaces that extends $\sigma$.

steps.slogan: Apply the nondegenerate case to $\sigma_1$ to extend $\sigma$ to all of $V$.
steps.detail: By step 2, $\sigma_1$ extends to an isometry $\tau$ of $V$. An isometry of a finite-dimensional nondegenerate space into itself is bijective, so $\tau\in O(V,q)$, and $\tau|_U=\sigma$.

concepts.c:nondegenerate-form: Nondegeneracy gives orthogonal splittings and the hyperbolic partners.
concepts.c:quadratic-form: The form $q$ is the structure that the extension must preserve.
concepts.c:isometry: The map $\sigma$ is an isometry that must extend.
concepts.c:orthogonal-group: The extension is an element of this group.
concepts.c:reflection-at-a-hyperplane: Reflections in anisotropic vectors are the basic isometries that move vectors.

source.note: The standard proof of the Witt extension theorem, as in T. Y. Lam, Introduction to Quadratic Forms over Fields, American Mathematical Society, 2005, Chapter I.

statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $S$ a finitely generated $R$-algebra, and $\mathfrak{p}$ a prime of $S$ at which $S$ is [quasi-finite](c:quasi-finite-morphism) over $R$. Let $S'$ be the [integral closure](c:integral-closure) of $R$ in $S$. Then some $r\in S'\setminus\mathfrak{p}$ makes the [localization](c:localization-of-a-ring) map $S'[1/r]\to S[1/r]$ bijective.

hypotheses.text: $R$ is a commutative ring and $S$ is a finitely generated $R$-algebra.
$S$ is [quasi-finite](c:quasi-finite-morphism) over $R$ at the prime $\mathfrak{p}$ of $S$: $\mathfrak{p}$ is isolated in its fibre.

conclusion: There is $r\in S'$ with $r\notin\mathfrak{p}$ such that $S'[1/r]\to S[1/r]$ is an isomorphism.

formal.difference: The declaration states exactly this algebraic form, as the property ZariskisMainProperty, with $R$ and $S$ in different universes. The geometric statement on birational morphisms of varieties, which the record's Wikipedia text describes, is not part of it.

proofs.name: Conductor argument and induction on generators
proofs.slogan: Reduce to a finite extension of a polynomial ring, use the conductor of one generator and quasi-finiteness to invert one element, and induct on the number of variables.
proofs.scope: The algebraic form of Zariski's main theorem (Stacks 00Q9). Zariski's original statement for a [birational morphism](c:birational-morphism) at a point of a [normal variety](c:normal-variety), and Grothendieck's form for quasi-finite separated morphisms, follow from it and are not proved here.

roles.why: Finite generation presents $S$ as a finite module over a polynomial ring in finitely many variables.
Quasi-finiteness at $\mathfrak{p}$ gives the coefficient outside $\mathfrak{p}$ and rules out strong transcendence.

steps.slogan: Replace $R$ by its integral closure $S'$ in $S$.
steps.detail: The algebra $S$ stays quasi-finite over $S'$ at $\mathfrak{p}$, and $S'$ is integral over $R$. So the property for $S'$ implies the property for $R$. Hence assume that $R$ is integrally closed in $S$.

steps.slogan: Treat the case where $S$ is generated by one element over $R$.
steps.detail: Write $S=R[X]/I$. Quasi-finiteness at $\mathfrak{p}$ gives some $g\in I$ with a coefficient $g_i\notin\mathfrak{p}$. Over $R[1/g_i]$ the polynomial $g$ is monic up to a technical adjustment, so $S[1/g_i]$ is integral over $R[1/g_i]$. Take $r=g_i$.

steps.slogan: Treat $S$ finite over $R[x]$ through the conductor of $x$.
steps.detail: Let $\mathfrak{f}$ be the conductor of $R[x]$ in $S$, the largest $S$-ideal inside $R[x]$. If $\mathfrak{f}\subseteq\mathfrak{p}$, then $x$ is strongly transcendental over $R$ in the reduced ring $S/\sqrt{\mathfrak{f}}$, which a going-down argument excludes. So some $c\in\mathfrak{f}\setminus\mathfrak{p}$ gives $R[x][1/c]=S[1/c]$, and step 2 applies to $R[x]$.

steps.slogan: Induct on the number of variables of the polynomial ring.
steps.detail: View $R[x_1,\dots,x_{n+1}]$ as $R'[x]$ with $R'=R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ and apply step 3 over $R'$ to get $r$. The subalgebra generated by the $x_i$, $r$ and the elements $r^ms$ for generators $s$ is finite over $R'$. The induction hypothesis applies to it, and transitivity gives the property for $S$.

steps.slogan: Present $S$ as a quotient of a polynomial ring and conclude.
steps.detail: A surjection $R[x_1,\dots,x_n]\to S$ is finite. Step 4 gives $r\notin\mathfrak{p}$ such that every $s\in S$ has $r^ms$ integral over $R$ for some $m$. So every element of $S[1/r]$ comes from $S'[1/r]$, and injectivity is clear.

concepts.c:quasi-finite-morphism: It is the hypothesis that gives the coefficient outside $\mathfrak{p}$ and excludes strong transcendence.
concepts.c:integral-closure: The ring $S'$ is the integral closure that the conclusion compares with $S$.
concepts.c:localization-of-a-ring: The conclusion says that two localizations agree.
concepts.c:birational-morphism: Zariski's original statement concerns birational morphisms, and is only named here.
concepts.c:normal-variety: Zariski's original statement is at points of normal varieties, and is only named here.

source.note: mathlib follows Stacks 00PI: of_adjoin_eq_top for one generator, of_algHom_polynomial with the conductor and strong transcendence, of_algHom_mvPolynomial by induction on the variables.

statement: Let $r\ge1$ and $k\ge0$. Take data $(B_1,B_2,I,J)$ with $B_i\in\mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C}^k)$, $I\in\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{C}^r,\mathbb{C}^k)$, $J\in\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{C}^k,\mathbb{C}^r)$, $[B_1,B_2]+IJ=0$, $[B_1,B_1^\dagger]+[B_2,B_2^\dagger]+II^\dagger-J^\dagger J=0$, and $(B_1-z_1,B_2-z_2,J)$ injective for every $z\in\mathbb{C}^2$. The monad of the data gives a bijection from such data modulo $U(k)$ onto the gauge classes of framed charge-$k$ $U(r)$ [instantons](c:instanton) on $\mathbb{R}^4$.

hypotheses.text: $r\ge1$ and $k\ge0$ are integers.

conclusion: Nondegenerate ADHM data modulo $U(k)$ correspond one to one with framed charge-$k$ instantons on $\mathbb{R}^4$ modulo gauge.

proofs.name: Donaldson's proof via bundles on the projective plane
proofs.slogan: Turn instantons into framed holomorphic bundles on $\mathbb{P}^2$, resolve them by a monad whose maps are the ADHM matrices, and pass to $U(k)$ by Kempf-Ness.
proofs.scope: An outline of Donaldson's proof for $U(r)$; the correspondence with holomorphic bundles and the monad theory rest on the cited work. Ideal instantons, where nondegeneracy fails, are excluded.

roles.why: The number $r$ is the rank of the framing and $k$ is the dimension of $V=H^1(E(-1))$.

steps.slogan: Replace instantons by framed holomorphic bundles on $\mathbb{P}^2$.
steps.detail: Compactify $\mathbb{R}^4=\mathbb{C}^2$ to $\mathbb{P}^2$ with line at infinity $\ell_\infty$. By a Hitchin-Kobayashi argument, framed charge-$k$ instantons correspond to stable [holomorphic bundles](c:holomorphic-vector-bundle) $E$ on $\mathbb{P}^2$ with $c_2=k$ and a trivialization $E|_{\ell_\infty}\cong\mathcal{O}^r$.

steps.slogan: Resolve $E$ by Beilinson's spectral sequence to get a [monad](c:beilinson-monad).
steps.detail: Stability and the framing give $H^0(E(-1))=H^2(E(-2))=0$. Beilinson's spectral sequence then writes $E$ as the cohomology of $V\otimes\mathcal{O}(-1)\xrightarrow{a}(V\oplus V\oplus W)\otimes\mathcal{O}\xrightarrow{b}V\otimes\mathcal{O}(1)$, with $V=H^1(E(-1))$ of dimension $k$, $W=\mathbb{C}^r$, $a$ injective, $b$ surjective and $ba=0$.

steps.slogan: Read the monad maps as the matrices $(B_1,B_2,I,J)$.
steps.detail: In coordinates, $a(z)=(B_1-z_1,\,B_2-z_2,\,J)$ and $b(z)=(-(B_2-z_2),\,B_1-z_1,\,I)$. The condition $ba=0$ is exactly $[B_1,B_2]+IJ=0$, and injectivity of $a(z)$ is the nondegeneracy. Monads up to $GL(V)$ match the data up to $GL(k)$.

steps.slogan: Replace $GL(k)$ by $U(k)$ and add the real moment-map equation.
steps.detail: Nondegenerate data have closed free $GL(k)$-orbits. By the Kempf-Ness theorem each such orbit contains exactly one $U(k)$-orbit solving $[B_1,B_1^\dagger]+[B_2,B_2^\dagger]+II^\dagger-J^\dagger J=0$. For solutions of this equation, $a(z)$ is injective iff $b(z)$ is surjective.

steps.slogan: Run the construction backwards from nondegenerate data.
steps.detail: The cohomology bundle of the monad is a stable holomorphic bundle with $c_2=k$ and a canonical framing at $\ell_\infty$, so it gives an instanton. The two constructions are inverse, since a monad is determined up to isomorphism by its cohomology bundle.

concepts.c:instanton: Framed instantons are the objects that the data parametrize.
concepts.c:holomorphic-vector-bundle: Instantons become holomorphic bundles on $\mathbb{P}^2$, where algebraic geometry applies.
concepts.c:beilinson-monad: The monad packages the bundle as linear algebra data.

source.ref: S. K. Donaldson, Instantons and geometric invariant theory, Communications in Mathematical Physics 93 (1984), 453-460
source.note: The construction is due to M. F. Atiyah, V. G. Drinfeld, N. J. Hitchin and Yu. I. Manin, Construction of instantons, Physics Letters A 65 (1978), 185-187.

statement: Let $F\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}$ be a functor between [presentable](c:presentable-infinity-1-category) $(\infty,1)$-categories. Then $F$ has a right [adjoint](c:adjoint-functor) if and only if $F$ preserves small colimits, and $F$ has a left adjoint if and only if $F$ is [accessible](c:accessible-functor) and preserves small limits.

hypotheses.text: $\mathcal{C}$ and $\mathcal{D}$ are [presentable](c:presentable-infinity-1-category) $(\infty,1)$-categories.

conclusion: A functor between presentable $(\infty,1)$-categories has a right adjoint iff it preserves small colimits, and a left adjoint iff it is accessible and preserves small limits.

proofs.name: Representability of limit-preserving functors
proofs.slogan: Build the adjoint object by object from the representability theorem for presentable categories, then assemble the objects into a functor.
proofs.scope: An outline of Lurie's proof; the representability theorem and the pointwise criterion for adjunctions rest on the cited work. The ordinary adjoint functor theorem is the model.

roles.why: Presentability gives the representability theorem, compact objects, and accessibility of right adjoints.

steps.slogan: Show that adjoints preserve colimits or limits, and that right adjoints are accessible.
steps.detail: A left adjoint preserves colimits and a right adjoint preserves limits, since $\mathrm{Map}(Fc,d)\simeq\mathrm{Map}(c,Gd)$ turns them into limits of mapping spaces. A right adjoint $G$ between presentable categories preserves $\kappa$-filtered colimits for large $\kappa$, because $F$ preserves $\kappa$-compact objects, so $G$ is [accessible](c:accessible-functor).

steps.slogan: Represent limit-preserving functors on a presentable category by objects.
steps.detail: For presentable $\mathcal{C}$, a functor $\mathcal{C}^{op}\to\mathcal{S}$ to spaces is [representable](c:representable-functor) iff it preserves small limits. A functor $\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{S}$ is [corepresentable](c:corepresentable-functor) iff it is accessible and preserves small limits. The proof presents $\mathcal{C}$ as a localization of presheaves and uses Yoneda.

steps.slogan: Build the right adjoint object by object for a colimit-preserving $F$.
steps.detail: Fix $d\in\mathcal{D}$. Since $F$ preserves colimits, $c\mapsto\mathrm{Map}_{\mathcal{D}}(Fc,d)$ sends colimits in $\mathcal{C}$ to limits of spaces. Step 2 gives an object $G(d)$ with $\mathrm{Map}(Fc,d)\simeq\mathrm{Map}(c,G(d))$, as in the ordinary adjoint functor theorem.

steps.slogan: Build the left adjoint object by object for an accessible, limit-preserving $F$.
steps.detail: Fix $d\in\mathcal{D}$. The functor $c\mapsto\mathrm{Map}_{\mathcal{D}}(d,Fc)$ preserves small limits, and it is accessible because $F$ is and $d$ is $\kappa$-compact for some $\kappa$. Step 2 gives $L(d)$ with $\mathrm{Map}(L(d),c)\simeq\mathrm{Map}(d,Fc)$.

steps.slogan: Assemble the representing objects into an adjoint functor and combine both directions.
steps.detail: Objects $G(d)$ or $L(d)$ chosen for all $d$ extend to a functor with natural equivalences, by the pointwise criterion for adjunctions. With step 1 this gives both equivalences of the theorem.

concepts.c:presentable-infinity-1-category: Presentability supplies the representability theorem and compact objects.
concepts.c:adjoint-functor: The theorem decides when this relation exists.
concepts.c:accessible-functor: Accessibility is the extra condition for a left adjoint.
concepts.c:representable-functor: Limit-preserving presheaves are representable, which builds the right adjoint.
concepts.c:corepresentable-functor: Accessible limit-preserving functors are corepresentable, which builds the left adjoint.

source.ref: J. Lurie, Higher Topos Theory, Annals of Mathematics Studies 170, Princeton University Press, 2009, Corollary 5.5.2.9
source.note: The representability theorem is in Section 5.5.2, and the pointwise criterion for adjunctions in Section 5.2.

statement: Every finite-dimensional [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) over a field of characteristic $0$ has a [faithful](c:faithful-representation) finite-dimensional representation, that is, it embeds in $\mathfrak{gl}(V)$ for some finite-dimensional $V$.

hypotheses.text: $\mathfrak{g}$ is a finite-dimensional [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) over a field $k$.
The field $k$ has characteristic $0$.

conclusion: There is a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ and an injective Lie algebra homomorphism $\mathfrak{g}\to\mathfrak{gl}(V)$.

proofs.name: Harish-Chandra's construction
proofs.slogan: Embed the algebra in one whose nilradical complement has a faithful module, build a finite-dimensional module of the nilradical from its enveloping algebra, and tensor.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof; the Levi decomposition and the splitting of step 2 rest on the cited work. The statement is for characteristic $0$; Iwasawa's theorem covers positive characteristic.

roles.why: Finite dimension makes the nilradical finite dimensional, so $\mathfrak{n}'\cap I^N=0$ for some $N$ and $M$ is finite dimensional.
Characteristic $0$ gives the Levi decomposition, $[\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{r}]\subseteq\mathfrak{n}$ and the splitting of derivations.

steps.slogan: Split off a Levi factor and locate the nilradical $\mathfrak{n}$ of $\mathfrak{g}$.
steps.detail: The Levi decomposition gives $\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{s}\ltimes\mathfrak{r}$ with $\mathfrak{s}$ semisimple and $\mathfrak{r}$ the radical. In characteristic $0$, $[\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{r}]\subseteq\mathfrak{n}$, so $\mathfrak{g}/\mathfrak{n}\cong\mathfrak{s}\oplus\mathfrak{r}/\mathfrak{n}$ with $\mathfrak{r}/\mathfrak{n}$ abelian and central.

steps.slogan: Embed $\mathfrak{g}$ in an algebra $\mathfrak{g}'=\mathfrak{h}\ltimes\mathfrak{n}'$ with $\mathfrak{n}'$ nilpotent.
steps.detail: Following Harish-Chandra, adjoin commuting derivations that absorb the non-nilpotent part of the action of $\mathfrak{r}$ on $\mathfrak{n}$, and enlarge $\mathfrak{n}$ to a nilpotent ideal $\mathfrak{n}'$. The subalgebra $\mathfrak{h}\cong\mathfrak{g}'/\mathfrak{n}'$ is built from $\mathfrak{s}$ and an abelian part, so it has a faithful representation $V\ne0$.

steps.slogan: Give the nilpotent algebra $\mathfrak{n}'$ a faithful finite-dimensional module.
steps.detail: Let $I$ be the augmentation ideal of the [universal enveloping algebra](c:universal-enveloping-algebra) $U(\mathfrak{n}')$. Because $\mathfrak{n}'$ is [nilpotent](c:nilpotent-lie-algebra), a PBW basis adapted to the lower central series gives $\mathfrak{n}'\cap I^N=0$ for large $N$. Then $M=U(\mathfrak{n}')/I^N$ is finite dimensional and $\mathfrak{n}'$ acts faithfully, since $x\cdot1=x\notin I^N$.

steps.slogan: Let the complement $\mathfrak{h}$ act on $M$ through derivations.
steps.detail: Each derivation $D$ of $\mathfrak{n}'$ extends to $U(\mathfrak{n}')$ and maps $I$ into $I$, hence $I^N$ into $I^N$. So $D\cdot u=D(u)$ acts on $M$. Since $[D,L_a]=L_{D(a)}$, the module $M$ is a module for $\mathfrak{g}'=\mathfrak{h}\ltimes\mathfrak{n}'$.

steps.slogan: Tensor $M$ with $V$ and restrict to $\mathfrak{g}$ to get a faithful module.
steps.detail: Let $\mathfrak{g}'$ act on $V$ through $\mathfrak{g}'/\mathfrak{n}'\cong\mathfrak{h}$, and on $M\otimes V$ diagonally. If $d+a$ with $d\in\mathfrak{h}$, $a\in\mathfrak{n}'$ acts as zero on $1\otimes v$, then $a\otimes v+1\otimes dv=0$. Since $M=k1\oplus I/I^N$, both terms vanish, so $a=0$ and $d=0$. Restrict to $\mathfrak{g}\subseteq\mathfrak{g}'$.

concepts.c:lie-algebra: The algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ is the object that must be embedded in matrices.
concepts.c:faithful-representation: A faithful representation is the embedding in $\mathfrak{gl}(V)$ that the theorem gives.
concepts.c:universal-enveloping-algebra: The quotient of $U(\mathfrak{n}')$ by a power of its augmentation ideal is the faithful module.
concepts.c:nilpotent-lie-algebra: Nilpotency makes the filtration by powers of $I$ meet $\mathfrak{n}'$ trivially.

source.ref: N. Jacobson, Lie Algebras, Interscience Publishers, New York, 1962, Chapter VI (the theorem of Ado, after Harish-Chandra)
source.note: Jacobson presents Harish-Chandra's proof, which builds a faithful module from the enveloping algebra of the nilradical.
